meaning: From the same root as Iuppiter, the bright sky

pronunciation.approximation: YOO-noh, long ū and long ō.
pronunciation.note: Latin Iūnō carries two long vowels, and both are preserved in the restoration; the macrons follow Lewis & Short. Her name shares the deep root of iuvenis, "young" — the goddess of the vital force in its prime — which is why her festival, the Kalends, belonged to women at the height of their powers. Old Latin inscriptions write the name IVNO — the consonantal V of Iūnō that the alphabet later split from U.

domains.title: The Queen of Heaven
domains.subtitle: Marriage, the Mint, and the Watching Geese
domains.lead: Iūnō is not "Hēra with a Latin accent" but a sovereign in her own right: protector of women in every life-stage, keeper of the state's financial memory on the Capitoline, and the one goddess Rome's enemies learned to fear as the will behind the legions.

cards.name: Lucina
cards.desc: Iūnō Lucina, "she who brings to light" — the goddess women call in childbirth.

cards.name: Moneta
cards.desc: "The Warner" — her Capitoline title; Rome's mint stood in her temple, giving the world the word "money."

cards.name: The Geese
cards.desc: Her sacred geese that woke the Capitol in 390 BCE when the Gauls climbed by night.

cards.name: Regina
cards.desc: The Queen — third of the Capitoline triad with Iūpiter and Minerva, enthroned on the city's heart-hill.

symbols.name: The peacock
symbols.meaning: Her Argive bird — the hundred eyes of Árgos set in its tail

symbols.name: The diadem
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty; she rules by right, not by marriage alone

symbols.name: The goose
symbols.meaning: Vigilance — the alarm the dogs slept through

symbols.name: The lily
symbols.meaning: In later art, the flower of her maternity

mythology.lead: Roman Iūnō inherits Hēra's jealousy plots but outgrows them: in Rome she is less the wronged wife than the state's queen — a power that must be ritually persuaded, city by city, to change sides.

myths.title: Tantaene Irae
myths.text: The Aeneid's engine is her anger: Virgil asks whether heavenly minds can hold such wrath, and answers with seven books of her persecution of Aeneas — the storm off Carthage, the madness of the Italian women, the marriage of Lavinia delayed to blood. When she finally yields, she extracts a condition: the Trojan name shall perish, and only Roman remain. She loses the war and wins the peace.

myths.title: The Goddess Who Changed Sides
myths.text: Before Rome stormed Veii in 396 BCE, the general Camillus performed the evocatio — formally calling the enemy city's Iūnō Regina to abandon Veii for a finer temple in Rome. The Veientine statue, Livy says, nodded assent. Rome conquered Italy partly by inviting its goddesses to defect: Iūnō's transferability made her the instrument of empire's softest power.

myths.title: The Geese of the Capitol
myths.text: When the Gauls scaled the Capitoline cliff by night in 390 BCE, the watchdogs slept — but Iūnō's sacred geese heard them and raised such a clamour that Marcus Manlius woke and threw the first Gaul back down. Rome remembered: dogs were thereafter crucified annually, geese honoured — and Iūnō received the title Moneta, the Warner, beside whose temple the mint later stood.

myths.title: Matronalia
myths.text: On March 1, the old New Year, Roman matrons kept Iūnō Lucina's feast: husbands prayed for wives, slaves were feasted by mistresses, and the temple on the Esquiline — vowed after a plague of stillbirths — received the processions of flowering branches. It was Rome's Mother's Day and its recognition of women's collective religious power.

lore.syncretism: Her Etruscan form Uni was Rome's first loan: the Capitoline triad itself (Iūpiter, Iūnō, Minerva) is the Etruscan Tinia-Uni-Ménrva. Through evocatio she accumulated the identities of every conquered city's queen — Iūnō Caelestis of Carthage was worshipped in Rome after Carthage burned — and her African form survived into Augustine's polemics. In the Greek East she was simply Hēra again: the empire made her portable in both directions.
lore.culturalLegacy: Her titles became common nouns: "money" and "monetary" descend from the mint in Moneta's temple; June (Iūnius) bears her name on every calendar; "junoesque" still describes stately beauty. The evocatio — winning by inviting the other side's gods to defect — remains the strangest instrument in the history of religious warfare, and scholars cite it in every discussion of Roman imperialism's flexibility.
lore.extendedMeditation: Iūnō is the power that must be persuaded, never merely defeated. Rome's deepest political insight is carved into her story: that legitimacy — of marriage, of money, of the state — is not seized but transferred, and only by consent. Her geese still wake at night in every institution that survives by vigilance rather than force.
lore.archaeology: The temple of Iūnō Moneta stood on the Arx of the Capitol (349 BCE), where the church of Santa Maria in Aracoeli now rises; the mint's location beside it is the accepted explanation of her name's fortune. Veii's Portonaccio temple — the probable home of the defected Regina — preserves its Etruscan terracottas in the Villa Giulia. Inscribed curses and votives from her Italic sanctuaries (especially at Lanuvium, with its famous serpent cult) document her continuous worship from Latium's earliest towns.
